reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Presents with postprandial epigastric pain, early satiety, nausea, bilious vomiting and weight loss from proximal small-bowel obstruction
The third part of the duodenum is compressed between the superior mesenteric artery in front and the aorta behind, in the angle where the artery leaves the aorta
Loss of the mesenteric fat pad from significant weight loss narrows the aorto-mesenteric angle, so it is often triggered by weight loss, creating a vicious cycle
Symptoms may be relieved by lying prone, in the knee-chest position, or on the left side, which opens the aorto-mesenteric angle
Associations include rapid weight loss, prolonged bed rest, spinal surgery or bracing, and eating disorders
Contrast studies and cross-sectional imaging show duodenal dilatation with an abrupt vertical cut-off and a reduced aorto-mesenteric angle and distance
Initial management is nutritional restoration to rebuild the mesenteric fat pad, with surgery such as duodenojejunostomy reserved for refractory cases
reference.pathophysiology: Superior mesenteric artery syndrome results from compression of the third part of the duodenum in the narrow angle between the superior mesenteric artery and the aorta. Normally a pad of mesenteric and retroperitoneal fat holds the artery away from the aorta, keeping the aorto-mesenteric angle wide enough for the duodenum to pass. Marked weight loss, catabolic states or altered spinal anatomy reduce this fat cushion, narrowing the angle and trapping the duodenum. The resulting partial obstruction causes proximal dilatation, vomiting and further weight loss, which in turn worsens the compression in a self-perpetuating cycle.
additionalDifferentials: Peptic ulcer disease with gastric outlet obstruction
additionalInvestigations: Upper gastrointestinal contrast study showing duodenal dilatation with abrupt cut-off
CT or MR angiography measuring the aorto-mesenteric angle and distance
Upper endoscopy to exclude mucosal and obstructing lesions
Nutritional assessment including weight and body-mass index
Investigations to exclude gastroparesis and other dysmotility
redFlags: Severe dehydration and electrolyte disturbance from persistent vomiting
Gastric or duodenal dilatation risking perforation or aspiration
Features of an underlying eating disorder requiring integrated care
reference.prognosis: Many patients improve with nutritional restoration and conservative measures; those with anatomical fixation or failure of conservative treatment may need surgery, which is generally effective.
pitfalls: Dismissing symptoms as functional or as an eating disorder without imaging the duodenum
Overlooking the syndrome as a complication of rapid weight loss or spinal treatment
Proceeding to surgery before an adequate trial of nutritional restoration
Failing to correct dehydration and electrolytes before intervention
